These are all private opinions of my own, which I have long wished to find an occasion to set down, so that an outsider too might understand a little of what the secret agent's frame of mind is like, and what he feels. To be sure, I cannot speak for every worker in the secret service; but at the least I have done such work all my life.

Around the time of the war of resistance, and above all in that year or two after I came to Shanghai, we did in truth "kill" too many men. Judged from the standpoint of the work, this had, of course, a certain value that may be reckoned up; but it was after all no fine thing to boast of, and there is naturally no call to take any pride in it.

I said in the preface to this book that, by an incomplete count, over the course of two years the "Shanghai District" sanctioned more than a hundred traitors great and small, killed more than forty armed Japanese officers and men, and besides these wrecked enemy military installations and burned military stores in more than fifty separate actions—among which, of course, there must also have been dead and wounded. My purpose was only to give some notion of the substance of it, with no thought of vaunting. And I said too, hiding nothing, that on our own side, counting only the personal sacrifices of the working comrades—those who gave their lives for the country, those crippled under torture, those thrown into prison—the total also came to more than two hundred. And so I once quietly let out what was in my heart, saying: "Action and sabotage can never be wholly free of burning and killing; and even I myself sometimes feel a reluctance in my heart."

Speaking of that "reluctance"—it is a real thing, and by no means said merely to sound well. I have a good friend who was once a commander of troops and fought in the field. One year, on the firing line, in a state of standoff between two armies, at the midnight hour he suddenly heard a subordinate outside the door calling to report; and when the man was summoned in and he listened closely, it turned out they had taken a "spy." He had the man brought in at once for questioning, but to his surprise the fellow was iron-hard and would not open his mouth—would not answer a single word. In that year my friend was only a little over thirty, full of hot blood and quick of temper; his anger flaring in an instant, he drew his pistol, leveled it at the man's skull, and said in a loud voice: "I ask you once more; if you will not answer honestly, I will shoot you dead." Truly a heart of iron and steel, worthy to be called a brave man—yet this fellow closed both his eyes, with all the air of one who held life and death beyond his care. That set my friend's temper off; he squeezed the trigger, two shots rang out, and sure enough the man was killed on the spot at the foot of the steps. A thing of this kind leaves a brand on the mind, and one may imagine how deep it goes. And so in the year he turned eighty, chatting with me, he said: "I have no regret in my whole life save that one time, when in a moment's passion I killed a man; fifty years on it still weighs on my heart, and I have never been able to forget it."

For that matter, to kill a man or two on the battlefield, whether with cause or not—especially in those years—was reckoned as nothing at all; yet it depends on the man it is laid upon. Some kill men like so much grass, unmoved; others, like my good friend, can never set it aside their whole life long.

Now to speak again of ourselves. By "ourselves" I mean myself and my comrades; and in truth none of us was fond of killing, still less could we be called bloodthirsty, much less men who took killing for a pleasure. The one and only reason we could not but kill was for the sake of "waging war." Everyone knows there is no fighting without men dying.

However others may see it, I for my part have always felt that a man in war and a man in times of peace differ greatly. The man of peacetime, under the protections of his rights, may be raised up as sacred and inviolable; the man in war is no more than a stone, a stick of wood, an implement for striking the other side, a moving target to be struck. Seen thus, a man's worth as a living being is cheapened by war, pared thin. This is why there is the saying, "Better a dog in a time of peace than a man in a time of chaos"—words spoken from the depths of feeling.

War is no clever thing; yet war has been with us since ancient times, and down to this present day of 1984 there are still a great many places in the world where wars go on. Yet to say that war is a foolish thing would not be quite right either. To leave the rest aside and take only the eight-year war against Japan: it was surely a sacred war against invasion, a war for survival, one that had to be fought, one for which we were prepared even to be shattered like jade, come what might. From this it may be seen that the subjective factors of war—the rise or fall of the nation, the survival or extinction of the race—are what drive and decide a people to fight at any cost.
To say it over again, and lay it down in broad terms: war has its own logic of inevitability. Limited as my grasp is, I am not yet fit to discourse on such matters.

The plain fact is this: since we had taken up secret-service work, and had run into a war besides, all we could do was follow the current and do what we ought to do. As for whether we "ought" or "ought not," there seems to have been no great choice in the matter.

The secret operatives under the leadership of Mr. Dai Yunong laid very great stress on action work, and this too may be explained as a policy. It had its own particular background of the times, and could not have been otherwise. Thus he once said, with emphasis: "Nothing less than a great shedding of blood will chill the enemy's heart." These words are found in a telegram he sent me, of which the original text runs: "The failure of the Wang affair last time (note: this refers to the sanction of Wang Kemin at Beiping in the twenty-seventh year) was in truth brought about by our action comrades' want of composure and of a resolve to die. Henceforth action must be undertaken with a determination to die, our whole strength gathered and staked upon a single throw; for nothing less than a great shedding of blood will chill the enemy's heart and exalt the resisting spirit of our race. When the deed is done there shall be a heavy reward; I beg you to use it to spur on the comrades."

By "a great shedding of blood" is meant not only making the enemy bleed, but that we too must not grudge shedding much of our own; the sense of that blood-shedding is lofty and deep, and hard to lay down in a definition. I take it to mean: kill a few more of the enemy, sacrifice a few more comrades, but only so as to bring about a positive effect—success, of course, is best, yet within failure too there is a success of its own. I do not know whether this is a fitting reading of it or not.

Writing to this point, I am put in mind of a story. Some say that in the early days, inside the "Juntong Bureau," the old saw "one general's fame is built on ten thousand rotting bones" was greatly shunned, so that among the comrades no one cared to speak the line. I count myself an old comrade of the "Juntong," but because my days were mostly spent on outside duty, I do not know whether there really was such a thing within. On inquiry, this proves to be from a Tang poem, "The Year Jihai," by Cao Song, which runs: "The rivers and hills of the water country are drawn into the maps of war; / by what means shall the common folk take joy in gathering wood and grass? / I pray you, sir, speak not of the deeds that win a marquisate: / one general's fame is built on ten thousand rotting bones." The whole poem is pitched in a low key and might well breed a sinking of the will; in that time of stirring up a soaring morale, it was indeed not very suitable. Still, as for "one general's fame is built on ten thousand rotting bones"—it is the same in all ages and all lands, the truth of the matter being just so, and no empty word.

Those who hold the policy in hand—in any organization it is for the most part the affair of the highest tier; in the case of the "Juntong Bureau," two or three men to assist and one man to decide, and that is all. The chiefs of an outside unit—a district or a station—are neither at the top nor at the bottom; they are executors who come to knowledge late, who do not fully understand the whole of the policy and its guidelines, and who, in seeking to keep step with their superiors, must rely wholly on their own guesswork. If their line of march is trodden just right, falling exactly into the rut, that is counted correct; a single step too far ahead or behind, and lightly they meet with sarcasm and a dressing-down, heavily they may find the blame more than they can bear.

This is something I came only slowly to see, many years after the fact; how others felt I never earnestly put forward to exchange views upon, and so of course no common conclusion was reached. Let it be set down, then, that I was oversensitive.

When I was district chief at Shanghai I was just past thirty, very green; I had my schemes, but did not know how to put them to use. Among colleagues there was no need for any of that; toward superiors, cautious and circumspect as I was, I still went with my heart in my mouth—how should I dare put forward any clever notions? And in truth, being a simple sort, I thought only of doing the work laid on my shoulders well, and had not the leisure even to make any plan for myself. Say it and it may be hard to believe, but from that time on I had no wish to rise in office and change my cap of rank; I had not even the will to climb. What I longed for and turned over in my mind day and night was how to set our own camp in an order firm as a rampart of iron, and to grapple with the enemy and the puppets to the end. As for when this war might at last be over—that I never so much as thought of.

It was, I think, around the end of the twenty-ninth year into the beginning of the thirtieth, when the work of the "Shanghai District" was daily more active and stood at its very peak, that my friend Hu Yongquan counseled me, saying: "Shanghai is, after all, no place to linger; I think it best to quit while you are ahead." He spoke, to be sure, out of goodwill, but I could not take it in. Besides, it did not rest with me: if a superior bade me stay, I could not go though I wished to; and the day a superior transferred me away, I should not dare stay a single day. He was an outsider—how should he know all these rules? And my own mind ran just contrary to his: I had no wish to be moved, and was very willing to stay on without limit, for I was in the thick of it and going strong. And here is a thing I am not afraid to say for all the laughter it may draw: to be the head of an outside unit, with an absolute power of command, could well satisfy that craving to dominate that all men share; and moreover, though one turned about only within a patch of ground that could not be smaller, there was still in it a freedom and an ease of its own.

Let the words above be taken as a fit of the moment. To go on: I had best speak more deeply of the meaning of "action work," and of its workings for good and for ill. This is wholly a view of my own, standing for nothing, and able to stand for nothing. It may here and there not wholly agree with the views Mr. Dai held; but as these are all old sayings of some decades ago, a few words more will do no harm.

In the "Long Prologue" to my whole book Nameless Heroes, I gave, in the passage on why we did "action work," an explanation to this effect: "We have always striven for the rule of law; when a citizen breaks the law there are statutes to meet it, so why not proceed through judicial process and fix his guilt by law—why must special means be used to sanction him?" Our correct answer to this question is: "Because the difference of place and setting made it impossible to exercise judicial power; or because, bound by unequal treaties between nations and stripped of extraterritorial jurisdiction, we could not, in order to safeguard the interests and security of the state, sit and watch the vermin of the nation range free beyond the law, sheltered under the enemy's wing, and even, leaning on foreign force, carry on their wicked traffic in ruining the people—and so we could not but adapt to the needs of reality and take this course resolutely."

Let me use as illustration the actual instances of "action work" I have taken part in or directed. Their time falls only around the war of resistance, that is, within the ten years from the twenty-second year of the Republic to the end of the thirtieth; their place, only in those special settings not under our government's rule or administration. To put it more concretely, these include the "Legation Quarter" at Beiping, the British, French, and Japanese concessions at Tianjin, and the International Settlement and French Concession at Shanghai; while as for Hanoi in French Annam, that was foreign soil, and the situation there was more special still. Beyond these, there were the fallen zones amid the ongoing war of resistance. As for the facts of these things, though they have been set out in full in the first and second parts of this book, there is no harm in offering a reminder of them here as follows:

In the spring of the twenty-second year, Japanese imperialism, having seized our Northeast, was pressing hard to plunder North China besides. The washed-up warlord Zhang Jingyao, former military governor of Hunan, at the instigation of the Japanese army slipped into Beiping to plot mischief. Though we knew perfectly well he lay hidden in the legation district, the "Legation Quarter," we still could not go and arrest him. What was to be done?

In the winter of the twenty-third year, the wanted man Ji Hongchang—a former general of the Northwest Army who had once been chairman of Ningxia province—used the name of resisting Japan to band with the Communists in the Chahar and Rehe region, raising an armed force on a great scale and turning his guns about to make open war on the national army; and though he later surrendered and was taken, he escaped en route while being escorted under guard. When this Ji slipped away to Tianjin and, under cover of the concessions, openly fomented disorder, could we let him run wild?

In the winter of the twenty-fourth year, Yin Rugeng, formerly administrative inspector of the Luan-Yu region of Hebei province, at the urging of the Japanese warlords betrayed the state and went so far as to usurp the title of an "East Hebei Anti-Communist Autonomous Committee" at Tongxian, leaning on foreign force to seize more than twenty counties and towns of East Hebei—truly a monkey dressed up as a man—and everything he did was the traitorous, people-harming business of "colluding with a foreign country." Though the government issued an express warrant for his arrest, there was no way to bring him to book; and to seek to bind him by the law—what then was to be done?

In the spring of the twenty-seventh year, Beiping having already fallen, the puppet North China regime headed by Wang Kemin and propped up by the Japanese army was aiding the tyrant and working its perverse course. Our brave comrades, braving ten thousand perils, dealt it a heavy blow under the enemy's and puppets' tight guard. This bold deed split the very stones and startled the heavens—who shall say it was not fitting!

From the end of the twenty-seventh year into the beginning of the twenty-eighth, Wang Jingwei issued his "Yan telegram," actually answering to the beck of the Japanese warlords and shaking the very foundations of the resistance. The blow at Hanoi was, I think, a most painful decision; while Wang's further setting up of a separate puppet government was folly of the extreme. Though the debate over this affair has not ceased to this day, still, done is done—so let right and wrong be clearly judged.
The many facts listed above are enough of themselves to show why action had to be taken.

In the stretch of time from the autumn of the twenty-eighth year to the winter of the thirtieth, our action work in Shanghai went forward with a fierce and thoroughgoing vigor: the number of those sanctioned grew, while their general standing dropped. This was by no means wanton killing, but the carrying out of a policy laid down by our superiors, the basic aim of which was to establish our renown, in the hope of producing a deterrent effect.

There is no sudden storm of wind and rain but carries dust and sand along with it; and when the cases of action grew many, to say that every single target was a wretch beyond all pardon, with nothing in him to be forgiven, would not be absolutely true either. We too were men of flesh and blood; and since I have come to this point, let me set down a feeling of the heart.

A supreme commander of the three armies, at a single word of command, may see thousands upon thousands turned to ashes; and he, I believe, is fighting the enemy with all his might, the more the better. Because he does not in the least know whether it is Zhang the Third or Li the Fourth who dies or is hurt, there is no burden on his mind. It is not so with action work: every target is a fixed man, and though one goes about it in fear and trembling, dreading any error, one still cannot say there is never a mishap. And once a mishap befalls, then, apart from the responsibility, how is the conscience to bear it?

Among the comrades, those who had directed or carried out action work would now and then, in conversation, touch on this very question; and for the most part they were unwilling to speak of it deeply. In such a case the reasons are of course complex, but I dare say there was always in it some measure of unease. Taking only the things I myself have been through, they are already enough to leave a man abashed; and if one thinks on them a little more, then it is far more than mere abashment.

In "Rooting Out Traitors in the North," in the case of sanctioning the Communist bandit Ji Hongchang, the target was Ji alone; yet who could have foreseen that the one who took the bullet and died would be Liu Shaorang. Just where the error lay we have gone over in every possible way, but never to this day have we found the right answer. And there is another matter—the identity of the dead man Liu Shaorang: only after checking did we learn that he was a representative sent by the Southwest faction to Tianjin to take part in anti-central activities. Now, between the Southwest and the central authorities there had long been many storms; and mixed in this way, was it not that the center had killed a man of the Southwest? In truth, beforehand we had known nothing at all of Liu Shaorang's going to Tianjin to join the "Chinese People's Anti-Fascist Grand Alliance," nor had we ever received any order to sanction Liu Shaorang; and through this crossing of wires a graver misunderstanding could very well have come about.

And there is more. One year in Shanghai I met my friend Mr. He in the street; each of us knew the other's inside story, and so with nothing held back we fell to talking over old times. As the talk went on, it turned out that the very Mr. Liu Shaorang who had died at the Guomin Hotel in Tianjin was my friend He's father-in-law. How awkward that was. Though I had done nothing wrong, still I could not but feel I had let my friend down.

Another matter befell in Shanghai in the thirty-third year. One day I went to the "Yu Xiangqin Law Office" on Mohawk Road to see my friend Yu Xiangqin on some business—not to bring a lawsuit. The writing-room was upstairs, and behind it was a small parlor kept especially for friends to "attend to matters"—sometimes for a chat, sometimes for a game of cards, and further as a place for "confidential counsel." That day there was another man present whom I did not know, and Yu Xiangqin introduced him to me, saying: "This is the lawyer Zhang Fayao; we are partners." Then at once he added a word: "You will know, old fellow, that Lawyer Zhang's father is that renowned figure of the Shanghai scene, Zhang Xiaolin, old Zhang—

Well, hearing this far I was already ill at ease, and my fear was that Zhang Fayao might blurt out a line like: "So it was you, sir, who was behind my father's murder." At such a moment, though I could have spoken a few righteous and forceful words, it would after all have been no pleasant thing for anyone.

In the first month of the seventy-third year, my old comrade in adversity Sheng Yu (Liyue) invited me for a talk. Sheng Liyue and I shared hardship together in Shanghai and Hangzhou for more than two years and got on very well; we may be said to have had no small friendship. In Taiwan he was a university professor, a tax-and-finance expert, a noted accountant; each of us had his own circle of life, and our comings and goings were not close. That he asked to see me must have been with some purpose. In fact, before we had even met, I already knew what he wished to speak of.
He knew, and I knew, that in the several decades gone by we had never once opened up and talked of this affair. This time, it had to be spoken of.
Yu Yefeng was Sheng Liyue's father-in-law; at the time of Yu's death Sheng was not yet married. Of course, the affairs of the Yu household Brother Liyue would naturally know far better than I.

By Brother Liyue's account to me: "My father-in-law did indeed go to Hong Kong, escorted there by Wang Xiaolai, chairman of the Shanghai General Chamber of Commerce. In Hong Kong my father-in-law saw Mr. Du, but the manner of it was rather cold. As for just what they talked of, that cannot be known. And as for the outside talk that my father-in-law had met Mr. Dai Yunong, that is likely mere hearsay."

Brother Liyue said gravely: "The chairman of the Shanghai General Chamber of Commerce was Mr. Wang Xiaolai. My father-in-law was never chairman of the 'Shanghai General Chamber of Commerce.'" On this point I did not, on the spot, argue it out with Brother Liyue. Only after I had returned did I check further: that "Shanghai General Chamber of Commerce" of Wang Xiaolai's had existed before the war, and after Shanghai fell it still continued on. Beyond it, was there yet another, a new "Shanghai General Chamber of Commerce"? I had a mind to go and seek a more satisfying answer.

Brother Liyue said again: "My father-in-law had many businesses and no small number of acquaintances, but he never touched on politics; that talk of his joining a 'New Asia Peace Promotion Association' is likely not the fact."

As to the relation between Yu and Zhang, Brother Liyue also had an explanation, saying: "Zhang Xiaolin called my father-in-law elder brother; in early years it was my father-in-law who had drawn him to Shanghai, and that he could lord it in Shanghai he owed in no small part to my father-in-law…"

Brother Liyue said with feeling: "My father-in-law never held any puppet office, and there was in truth no fact of his colluding with the enemy; for the government to treat him so was rather too much."
In the ordinary way, such was Brother Liyue's character that he would not have said so much; from which one may see that he spoke indeed out of deep feeling.

At the time we were at table, at a meal; to talk of these things while eating was really not very fitting. I remember I once said to Brother Liyue: "Save that I cannot disown my own self, in the matter of your father-in-law I am willing to do whatever you wish." Why? Because Brother Sheng Liyue is a true gentleman.

Besides this, there is much else that is hard to bear. That action work should drag others into the parting of wife from husband, the breaking of families and the loss of lives—such things too there were, and to think of them is to feel the sin of it.

The sanction of Fu Xiao'an by Zhu Sheng was in some respects unlike Lin Huaibu's killing of Zhang Xiaolin: in the Zhang case the whole course of events holds, to this day, points of doubt that cannot be resolved, whereas the Fu case is clear in its every stage, and though some details were left out, there is not a single contradiction in it.

The "Second Action Brigade" had beforehand sent in a written report, setting out in concrete terms that it had already "got through" to a servant at Fu's side, one named Zhu Sheng, who was awaiting his chance to act. This term "got through" is a piece of the trade's jargon; the general procedure of it is that, once the target is fixed upon, through a face-to-face contact between the two sides' key go-betweens, or between the principals themselves, each states his wishes, and mutual assent is reached—the final conclusion so arrived at is what is called "getting through." To put it more plainly: once the men of the Second Brigade had made connection with Fu Xiao'an's servant Zhu Sheng, the Second Brigade judged that to have Zhu Sheng await his chance to sanction Fu Xiao'an could not be more fitting, while Zhu Sheng for his part understood that the party he was in contact with (the Second Brigade) was the very party he had been seeking; and when the Second Brigade put to Zhu Sheng their wish that he "do away with this Fu," Zhu Sheng, without the least constraint, wholly agreed. Thereupon Zhu Sheng also expressed a hope that, the deed done, he might receive a reward of fifty thousand yuan, and the Second Brigade likewise promised it. And so this matter was "settled."

The Fu case had two chief distinctions. First, the demand for a reward to be paid beforehand—this, among the action work I directed, should count as the first of its kind. Only, Zhu Sheng himself put it as "after the deed is done"; and moreover, what he obtained was merely a verbal promise, with no concrete guarantee of any sort. This again was rather unlike a purely Western sort of cash bargain; that is to say, there was mixed in it a good measure of the sense that "a traitor is one whom any man may put to death." Second, it was a case of striking sparks at the first touch—both parties willing, with no persuasion urged and no deceit practiced; and this, I should say, was the most practical element of the case's success.

Fifty thousand yuan, in the Shanghai of the twenty-ninth year, was by any reckoning no small sum: used to buy rice, it came to several thousand piculs; laid out on property—take an ordinary apartment flat in the concessions for an example—it was enough to buy several such buildings; and if one wished to set up some trade, so long as the scale were not too large, it was in no way too little to found a business.

In the Second Brigade's report a special request for instructions was made on this very point; and I, seeing that the Brigade had already given its promise, expediently agreed to it, without at the time considering what should be done if my superiors would not allow it. Yet why then did I not forward the Second Brigade's request to my superiors for a ruling on its original terms? I feared to lose the moment, and dreaded besides that complications might branch out from it; if I put it to my superiors in plain words—that this man asked for a reward of fifty thousand yuan to be paid once the deed was done—I felt always that, the thing being without precedent, I did not know how best to phrase it; and on the other hand there was mixed in, in some measure, a competitive wish to show that I had decision and could carry a burden. Of course, I had my reckoning too: that once it truly succeeded, there would be no question of my superiors' upholding the promise we had already given.

I recall too that the Second Brigade's report, though signed as usual by the brigade commander Zhao Sheng, stated within it that the beginning and the progress of this affair had been wholly managed by the sub-brigade commander, Comrade Chen Mo. This too was the first time I formed any impression of Chen Mo.

There was talk outside that Fu's servant Zhu Sheng and the gatekeeper of the Du household were fellow-townsmen from Shandong who had long been on visiting terms, and that it was thereby the connection had been made, and afterward the matter opened up between them. Whether in fact it was so, the Second Brigade's report as passed up to us did not touch upon this point.

Writing to this point, a thought suddenly comes to me: that at the time, whenever a matter touched on the Du household, the Second Brigade would always pass it over with a single stroke, sketchy and not detailed; and only now do I understand that it was not that the Second Brigade's comrades meant to fudge, but that their aim was to keep the Du household's connection perfectly clear of it, lest it be tainted by any right or wrong. In this there was plainly a principle at work. It was only that I was too green to grasp so much. These are but a couple of idle remarks, yet they too are the plain fact.

To speak again of Zhu Sheng's carrying out the sanction of Fu Xiao'an. The Second Brigade's report reached the District headquarters not long after the Zhang Xiaolin case, about the last third of the ninth month; and thereafter, through two or three exchanges of query and reply, it was already early in the tenth month.

The District secretary, Brother Qi Qingbin, in handling any case whatever, never let a change of expression show; it was very hard to read from his face the attitude he held, and so it was with the Fu Xiao'an case too. On the matter of paying a reward of fifty thousand yuan once the deed was done, he expressed no opinion; I once asked him, and he said: "A promise given is to be kept; where is the problem in that?"

When Zhu Sheng would act was fixed by no set term; it truly depended on the chance. Without a chance one could not force it; with a chance one must not let it slip—the whole of it hung on Zhu Sheng alone. Beforehand we more than once relayed a query to Zhu Sheng as to what support he needed, and he said: "There is nothing you can lend a hand with." That being so, we could only wait in earnest expectation. Some too had asked: "Why do you not contrive a way, make a chance?" To my shame, we had not that skill.

The Double Tenth passed like any ordinary day, for our circumstances did not allow us to celebrate. Who could have foreseen that on the very day after the Double Tenth—the morning of the eleventh of the tenth month of the twenty-ninth year—the courier brought back the Second Brigade's written report.

The report was written in plain script on a small slip of paper, with no cipher and no code words, and not even an envelope added. This little slip was far smaller than an ordinary sheet of lined letter-paper; folded and folded again into a long strip, some three or four tenths of an inch wide and seven or eight inches long, and then plaited into three squares joined in a row—which signified a "most urgent item." By the rule, the courier could only pass it on as fast as he might, and was on no account permitted to open it for a single glance.

Before I had even reached the first office, the District secretary, Brother Qi Qingbin, had long since opened this urgent dispatch, and had at the same time drafted the telegram to be relayed to our superiors, waiting only for me to look it over, whereupon it could be sent off at once.

The content of the Second Brigade's report was very simple, the main of it being that Zhu Sheng had completed his mission and was now safely out of danger, and was at that moment being escorted by Comrade Chen Mo and others toward Pudong; once he had arrived and been settled, a fuller report would follow.

Having read the report through, Qingbin and I exchanged a glance and a faint smile, each of us seeming to feel a moment's lightening at a piece of work brought off; but it lasted a very short while, for the thought of the many, many unfinished tasks heaped before our eyes drew us taut again in spite of ourselves.

So I asked Brother Qingbin to reply to the Second Brigade with words of comfort and encouragement, and to charge the Brigade to take proper care of the patriot Zhu Sheng, sending him, when circumstances allowed, to the rear as the fitter course; or, should he have some other refuge, to let it be as he wished.

Besides this, by word of mouth I told Brother Qingbin that on the matter of the fifty thousand yuan reward already promised, once the Second Brigade's follow-up report had reached the District and been fully confirmed, I would send a separate telegram to Mr. Dai for his ruling; and when the draft was written I would ask him to look it over and see whether it were fitting.

The killing of Fu Xiao'an took place a little after three in the morning of the eleventh; the morning papers seem all to have missed it, but the evening papers carried it in full, and some newspaper offices had, as early as around noon, posted "extras" at the busy crossings of the several streets. That this thing was true beyond all doubt was now past question. Around four in the afternoon the Second Brigade's report also came: this was after Comrade Chen Mo had escorted Comrade Zhu Sheng to Pudong and seen him settled and returned to the concessions, reporting by word of mouth to the brigade commander Zhao Sheng, who then put it in writing and relayed it to the District headquarters.

What the written report said and what the papers carried were roughly alike; in the fine points, what the papers depicted was more detailed still than what the report set out. This piece of news was in all the Shanghai papers of the day—dailies and evening papers, great papers and small—but it is a pity they can no longer be found; and now, by the kindness of Brother Pei Kequan, who obtained a clipping from the Chongqing Ta Kung Pao, its text runs as follows—

From the Chongqing Ta Kung Pao of the twelfth of the tenth month of the twenty-ninth year, a Central News Agency dispatch from Hong Kong dated the eleventh, from a Shanghai report: "On the morning of the eleventh, within the enemy garrison zone of Hongkou, a great murder took place; the slain was the puppet Shanghai mayor, the traitor Fu Xiao'an, who died of his grievous wounds on the spot. When the news got abroad, there was not a soul in the whole city who did not cheer.

"Inquiry finds that the place where the traitor Fu Xiao'an was slain was his residence at No. 2, Lane 26, Xiangde Road, Hongkou, very close to the Japanese Naval Landing Party, and ordinarily under a strict guard: besides some twenty-odd puppet guardsmen posted about the building, twelve White Russian bodyguards were hired for his protection, and when the traitor Fu slept, the bodyguards kept watch outside his bedchamber.

"On the night of the tenth, the traitor Fu feasted at the home of kin and friends in the French Concession, returning to his residence to sleep only at three in the morning of the eleventh. His concubine lodged in the rear chamber; toward four o'clock the concubine heard an unwonted sound, hurried forward to look, and found the traitor Fu with his face all bathed in blood: he had taken three knife-strokes in all—one on the eye, one on the chin, one on the neck—the neck-wound being the gravest, the head all but severed, the chin sliced away in a piece, the eyeball too near gouged out; breath was already gone, and the assassin had fled without a trace.

"The enemy, on being informed, sent men at once to investigate; judging that with the traitor Fu's gates so strictly kept an outsider could hardly have come and gone with ease, they searched the rooms and found that an old servant, one Zhu Sheng, alias Chen Zhongnan, had vanished. Besides throwing a special cordon and search over the households of the Hongkou district, the enemy dispatched men, together with the concession police, to search and arrest at Zhu's residence at a certain number on Nanking Road. According to those who shared the house: Zhu and his wife had moved away a week before, and where they had gone was not known.

"It is learned that Zhu was a Shandong man, forty-two years of age, hired by the traitor Fu in the sixteenth year of the Republic, when, being wanted by the national government, Fu took refuge in Dairen; he had followed the traitor Fu thirteen years, and after coming to Shanghai attended to the cleaning of the traitor Fu's bedchamber, at a monthly wage of twenty-two yuan.

"Zhu, after killing the traitor Fu, fled out of the gate by bicycle, and on the way met another maidservant, to whom he made the excuse that he had given notice and was going home. After the traitor Fu's killing the enemy and puppets were alike thrown into the utmost alarm and dread; besides telegraphing a report to the puppet Executive Yuan, they made strict search for the assassin, offering a reward of fifty thousand yuan, and the enemy further ordered the Nanjing–Shanghai trains halted, the better to search him out.

"The traitor Fu's corpse still lay within the residence, and when it would be coffined was as yet unfixed. The traitor Fu's given name was Zongyao, his courtesy name Xiao'an; he was sixty-nine years of age, a man of Ningbo in Zhejiang, and under the late Qing had held ——— (the characters are illegible). He had in succession been superintendent of the Jiangnan Shipbuilding Works, director-general of the government-run inland Waterworks Company of the Beijing government, supervisor of the Bank of China, superintendent of the Shanghai Mint, senior adviser to the State Council, chairman of the Shanghai General Chamber of Commerce, director-general of the China Merchants' Steam Navigation Company, chairman of the board of the China Commercial Bank, a director of the Ningpo Commercial Bank, resident Chinese manager at Shanghai of the American Bank Note Company, and chairman, concurrently vice-chairman of the board, of the Hanyeping Shareholders' Joint Association. In the sixteenth year of the Republic, for aiding Sun Chuanfang, he was put under warrant by the national government and fled to Dairen. On the sixteenth of the tenth month of the twenty-seventh year of the Republic he succeeded the traitor Su Xiwen as puppet mayor of Shanghai, and had held it now just two years. Day by day he played the tiger's cat's-paw, preyed on the townsfolk, sold out the nation and the race, and was content to be the enemy's running dog—one of the arch-villains among the pack of traitors.

"On the twenty-fifth of the eleventh month of the twenty-seventh year of the Republic he was once before set upon by an assassin: his bodyguard was shot dead, but the traitor Fu dodged and by luck escaped; this time he was at last stabbed to death—for the state a great traitor rooted out, for the race a chief criminal removed, at which there was not a soul in the whole nation but rejoiced with a glad heart; it may be called a comedy of congratulation amid the National Day festivities. And that the place where the traitor Fu was slain lay within the enemy army's sphere of power at Hongkou—where the enemy could not even protect one puppet of theirs—leaves them, of themselves, no pretext to lay against the concession side.

"Fu had a wife and a concubine; the wife, née ——, died of illness last winter, and the concubine, née Zhang, of North China stock, has now been raised to the first place. There was a son and a daughter, one of each; the daughter married Song Yougui, a manager of the China Commercial Bank, and the son, named Pingui, is chief auditor of the China & South Sea Bank, with nine sons and four daughters. The traitor Fu had been set to cross east to Japan on the twenty-fourth to attend the so-called East Asia Great-Cities League, but unexpectedly met his death ahead of the day."

This item of Central News Agency reportage above is the most detailed of the openly available material I have seen; and though I dare not call it the most accurate, I take it to be the closest to the facts as well. Let me now, drawing in other material besides, add and explain some points touched on in the report:

Fu's residence at Hongkou was not at all hidden; a passerby too could see that the one who dwelt within must be some "personage," for what ordinary common family could keep up such a "state"? Several units of the "Shanghai District" had gone to reconnoiter it, and all judged it hard to approach; and as for going at it by force, that was out of the question. As for the Japanese Naval Landing Party near the Fu house, that was no great matter: by our experience, in small affairs of no consequence they would not meddle.

The Fu family's guard corps was set up expressly to protect Fu, the puppet city government merely carrying them on its rolls for pay. This body of guards had not been drafted in from any peace-preservation corps or police bureau, and so bore a more particular charge and were correspondingly in earnest. As for the report's saying that twelve White Russian bodyguards besides were hired—that may have been so, or perhaps there were not so many. Still, inside and out, several dozen men was already enough to overawe.

As for its being said that even in his sleep at night there were men on watch outside—I doubt it; or if there were, it was not carried out strictly enough, else how could Zhu Sheng, having done the deed, still walk out from the scene bold as brass?

Concerning the feast on the night of the tenth at kin and friends' in the French Concession, the tales differ. One says: "One night, Fu Xiao'an, with a party of friends—Zhou Wenrui, Wei Jinsan, and the rest—was at the home of Sheng the Third, where on the spur of the moment they fetched the famous Yue opera (Shaoxing opera) actress Yao Shuijuan to play a scene from Interrogating the Husband, Demanding the Husband; in high spirits and merry, Fu did not return until after three in the morning." Another says: "On the night of the ninth of the tenth month, Fu Xiao'an rode in an armored motorcar to attend a banquet of the Japanese. When the feast broke up he went on to Sheng the Third's house, fetched on the spot the famous Yue opera actress Yao Shuijuan to perform Interrogating the Husband, Demanding the Husband before the wine, drank himself dead-drunk with a company of friends, and parted after the pleasure was full; returning home at three in the morning, he did not shut his door properly, but fell onto his bed and slept alone." Yet another differs a little, the gist being: "One winter, at about three past midnight, Fu Xiao'an had just come back from an engagement outside; old Zhu, as was his custom, brought up a bowl of stewed white fungus, but Fu put it off, saying he was too tired and would not have it." The common point of these three is that on this night Fu Xiao'an came home from outside very late indeed.

Besides the news reports, other material too says that Fu Xiao'an lived alone in a single room—that is, slept by himself in one chamber, not even sharing it with his wife. This point too gave Zhu Sheng no small convenience in striking.
As for the implement Zhu Sheng used, the reports give a knife or an axe; in the work report, what was used was an ordinary hatchet, no specially made article.

Of this patriot's name, several forms are seen in the material—Zhu Sheng, Zhu Sheng, Zhu Sheng, Zhu Shengyuan, and the like—only the Central News Agency saying he was also called "Chen Zhongnan," on what authority I do not know. In the work report received by the "Shanghai District," his name was "Zhu Sheng."
As to where on Fu Xiao'an's person the mortal wound was, the several papers differ too; of the bloody scene there is nothing worth depicting.

Whether Zhu Sheng had a dwelling on Nanking Road in the International Settlement, at the time we gave no heed. The report's saying that he had a wife who afterward moved off to parts unknown—to this too we paid no attention. According to the Central News Agency, Zhu Sheng was a Shandong man of forty-two; yet in many other reports he is called "old Zhu," which is hardly right—how can a man of forty-two be called an "old fellow"? The Central News Agency says that Fu, being under government warrant and taking refuge in Dairen in the sixteenth year of the Republic, hired Zhu Sheng as a servant, thirteen years in all, to see to the cleaning of Fu's bedchamber—what is commonly called a "valet"—and not the head cook of the kitchen that rumor made him.

A valet is more in keeping with reason than a head cook: in the great households of the old style, the head cook, when he had a word for the master, could only stand outside the door and enter when told to "come in," whereas the valet who waited on the master, being used to it, went in and out of the rooms as a matter of course.
After Zhu Sheng killed Fu Xiao'an he did indeed leave the scene by bicycle; of what followed, the executing unit has a separate report.

That the enemy and puppets should blockade and search was to be expected, and could not but harry the common people once again—this had become almost a fixed pattern—yet of our own men, not a single one, it may be said, was arrested on this account.

As for Fu Xiao'an's origins and career, the Central News Agency reported them in the greatest detail; and after we had read that long string of titles of his, the impression it gave us was that he had been a standard specimen of the old bureaucrat-cum-comprador. His ties with the Japanese were, of course, plainly laid in that one trip to Dairen. It is said that in Dairen Fu struck up friendships with no few Japanese, among them soldiers; that the Japanese later backed him to be "mayor of Shanghai" very likely had its root here.

There is a passage in the Central News Agency's report: "On the twenty-fifth of the eleventh month of the twenty-seventh year, Fu was once set upon by an assassin; his bodyguard was shot dead, but Fu himself escaped." Checking the date, it was just the fortieth day after Fu took up the office of puppet Shanghai mayor. Whether this was the doing of the previous "Shanghai District" I do not know, for at that time I was still in Tianjin.

On the matter of Fu's being put under government warrant in the sixteenth year of the Republic, the material says: "When the National Revolutionary Army in its Northern Expedition reached Jiangxi, Fu, in his capacity as director-general of the China Merchants' Steam Navigation Company (?), had dealings with Sun Chuanfang, commander-in-chief of the allied forces, and there was even talk of his tacitly consenting that 'all the river steamers be placed at his disposal.'" Whether this is true or not I do not know. There is another account: that the government afterward canceled the warrant against Fu, so that he could return to Shanghai, and that this was through Mr. Yu Qiaqing's putting in a good word for him. Matters of this kind breed many a conjecture; one may but let them pass for what they are worth. And to seek proof—there is the difficulty indeed.

Then who were the Japanese who backed Fu from behind? The intelligence material indicates that the one who backed Fu most strongly was Colonel Usui Kanzō, whose post was chief of the Eighth Section of the Japanese General Staff; from which it appears that this was no partiality of the Japanese side toward Fu, but a stratagem—what the Japanese call the working of "intrigue." Or one may say that Fu Xiao'an stood for Japanese interests. Even before the Wang puppet government was set up, Fu had taken the post of puppet Shanghai mayor; at that time it was called the "Great Way City Government," a purely Japanese-fostered traitor-puppet.

On the day after Fu Xiao'an's death, Mabuchi, chief of the reportage department (military spokesman) of the Japanese China Expeditionary Army General Headquarters (at Nanjing), made a statement as follows:

"The murderous outrage upon Shanghai Mayor Fu Xiao'an, in view of the importance of Shanghai on the road of New China's construction, is a matter of the utmost regret and of unbounded grief. Mayor Fu, who had offered his very life to the so-called revolutionary enterprise of the century, conceived as the peaceful building of the nation and the construction of the New Order in East Asia, had long been awake to all manner of untoward calamity, and so had a mind ever prepared for it; yet Greater Shanghai, which with a new mission and meaning after the war was to set forth afresh, now shows, whether economically, politically, or internationally, an advance by leaps and bounds, becoming the heart of New China, the feeler of the international situation, so that the city government's responsibility is graver still. That so great and famous a mayor should suddenly at this time be sacrificed is a loss not only to Shanghai but a great loss to all China.

"Looking back to when the calamities of war lay still heaped upon us: after the Great Way City Government was dissolved, he took up this weighty charge of Greater Shanghai's municipal affairs, overcoming every persecution and difficulty to form a sound administration, and lately even succeeded in having the Municipal Council return the land accounts, so that war-stricken Shanghai reached the prosperity of today—this indeed by the late mayor's self-sacrificing labor in his feeling for state and people, an achievement that may leave a bright page in the history of New China's construction. Why has the Chongqing regime to this day been unable to assassinate Mayor Fu; and what good influence does the assassination of Mayor Fu even now bring to the anti-Japanese camp? Of late, upon Japanese soldiers in uniform, and above all upon those shot dead—this has already happened twice—this too falls within the category of the Chongqing side's crimes of terror, a thing indeed never before seen.

"With the Japanese army's entry into Vietnam, and the three-Power alliance of Japan, Germany, and Italy, the new East Asian order with Japan as its leader has begun its mighty stride; disturbances of Chongqing's kind are truly not worth a glance. That the meritorious builders of East Asia should fall to Chongqing's benighted and murderous blade, so that many enterprises left unfinished become a pitiable sacrifice, is a thing to be lamented beyond all lamenting."

This statement above appeared in the Shanghai Xinshen Bao of the eleventh of the tenth month of the twenty-ninth year; the original text is thus, seeming coherent yet not quite so—I suppose it was rendered out of Japanese, and the translator perhaps a Japanese.

The "Great Way City Government" was the puppet "Shanghai City Government" under the puppet "Reformed Government" that the Japanese fostered after the fall of Shanghai; the previous puppet mayor was Su Xiwen.

Mabuchi's saying that "of late, upon Japanese soldiers in uniform, those shot dead…" refers to the "plan to strike the enemy" carried out by our "Shanghai District," set out in full in Chapter Seven of this book.

If one does not take the matter too gravely, and slackens the measure a little, and sets the two sides' responses side by side, there is in it a good deal worth pondering. The Central News Agency, standing for the right side, said: "Fu Xiao'an, day by day playing the tiger's cat's-paw, preyed on the townsfolk, sold out the nation and the race, was content to be the enemy's running dog, one of the arch-villains among the pack of traitors… this time at last stabbed to death—for the state a great traitor rooted out, for the race a chief criminal removed, at which there was not a soul in the whole nation but rejoiced with a glad heart."

The reportage department of the Japanese China Expeditionary Army, standing for the wrong side, said: "Mayor Fu, who had offered his very life to the so-called revolutionary enterprise of the century, conceived as the peaceful building of the nation and the construction of the New Order in East Asia… should suddenly at this time be sacrificed, a loss not only to Shanghai but a great loss to all China."

In truth, one Fu Xiao'an was of no account to begin with; there was nothing in the man worth taking. And now, roasted by these two—scorched by the one side and hoisted by the other—he seems really to have become a somebody. The affairs of this world are ever so.

The Fu case has one further distinction: on the face of it, it was no more than a servant's killing his master, with not the least political color to be seen; the strange thing is that in all the news reports, whatever their standpoint, they said with one voice that it was the doing of Chongqing elements, of the "Blue Shirt Society," of patriotic zealots—no one so much as suspected a feud avenged or a killing for gain. This too, I think, is what "renown" means.

Besides this, Fu's killing is written of too in the "Diary of Zhou Fohai," the entry being: "On the eleventh of the tenth month, waked by a telephone call at five o'clock: Shiqun reports that Mayor Fu Xiao'an of Shanghai was stabbed to death with a knife by a servant who had followed him a dozen years and more. The heart of man is unfathomable; it chills one to the bone." These few words have much of the air of the fox grieving over the dead hare.

Then Zhou wrote on: "Presently attended the Central Political Council. After it, briefly discussed with Mr. Wang the choice of a Shanghai mayor. Mr. Wang put forward Chu Minyi; I held for Gongbo, saying that a Yuan president holding a local post concurrently already had the precedent of Wang Yitang, and that Nanjing and Shanghai being so near, the going and coming most convenient, it would be no hard thing to attend to both. Mr. Wang thought so too. Presently went to the Ministry of Finance and dealt briefly with matters. In the afternoon returned to Shanghai; Shiqun and others went to the airfield to meet me, and reported the course of the Fu case, urging strongly that I take the mayoralty concurrently. I held it most unreasonable. He made it plain he was unwilling to have another come to Shanghai; if I could not hold it concurrently, he hoped for one who would absolutely heed my word—a thing that put me in real difficulty. Called on Gongbo, talked over how things stood since we had parted, and urged him to take the Shanghai mayoralty. He made it plain he was unwilling to be a local official, and put forward Siping in his stead; yet from the look of his meaning, he did not seem absolutely unwilling to come forward."
Let me first explain, so far as I know them, the several names and their puppet posts mentioned in the passage of Zhou Fohai's diary above:
"Shiqun" is Li Shiqun, the ruling man of the puppet Special Operations Headquarters, who not long after took over from Zhou Fohai as chief of police of the Wang puppet regime.
"Mr. Wang" and "Mr." are Wang Jingwei.
"Chu Minyi" is that big-bearded fellow who drove the carriage for Yang Xiuqiong; Wang counted him a trusted intimate, and at this moment he held the puppet post of foreign minister.
"Gongbo" is Chen Gongbo, at the time the puppet president of the Executive Yuan, Zhou Fohai being vice-president.
"Siping" is Mei Siping.

Fu Xiao'an's death seems also to have cleared an obstacle for the Wang puppet regime; for the Wang regime had early wished to replace Fu Xiao'an, but, hampered by the Japanese backing him, could do nothing. Now, with Fu Xiao'an dead and the Shanghai mayoralty fallen vacant, they at once fell to considering a successor.
Wang Jingwei's wishing to use Chu Minyi was wholly a placing of his own man; Chu Minyi was in fact truly not up to it.

Zhou Fohai's holding that Chen Gongbo should take the Shanghai mayoralty concurrently as president of the Executive Yuan was a wish to move Chen Gongbo aside, so that he himself, as vice-president, might exercise the president's powers—a scheme to lure the tiger from the mountain.

Li Shiqun in truth had designs on the Shanghai mayoralty too, but could not well say so openly, and therefore urged with all his might that Zhou Fohai hold it concurrently, longing for Zhou Fohai to say a word—"You had best come to it yourself." But little did Li Shiqun know that Zhou Fohai held his standing to be far too short for it.
Chen Gongbo's recommending Mei Siping in his stead was, on the other hand, sincere, for they were of one party to begin with. Yet Mei Siping too seems not to have been of much weight.

This pack, each with his own mask, made, when one looks at it, still but a scene from "Officialdom Unmasked." In the end it was Chen Gongbo who filled Fu Xiao'an's place and held the puppet Shanghai mayoralty concurrently.
The passage above concerns the subtle relation between the Fu Xiao'an case and the Wang puppet regime.
Next to speak again of the whereabouts of this Zhu Sheng.

After the sanction of Fu Xiao'an had been wholly confirmed, I sent in my own name a further telegram marked for Mr. Dai's personal decoding, the main of it being the hope that Mr. Dai would approve the fifty thousand yuan reward I had promised Zhu Sheng beforehand. Mr. Dai had said: "If, brother, you have any difficulty as to funds, do by all means telegraph me at any time; however hard-pressed I may be, I will surely find a way for you."

Not many days after the telegram was sent, Mr. Dai's reply arrived: for the whole case, a reward of seventy thousand yuan was granted—of which, besides the fifty thousand paid to Zhu Sheng as promised, a further twenty thousand was awarded to the Second Brigade. Of the fact that no ruling had been sought beforehand, not a word was said.

The "Shanghai District," besides passing the fifty thousand reward to the Second Brigade to be delivered to Zhu Sheng himself against his signed receipt, likewise paid the further twenty thousand to the Second Brigade by the general rule, to be distributed and then reported to the District for the record.

Chen Mo, having handed the fifty thousand reward to Zhu Sheng, further arranged for him to take a fishing boat out to sea, to land somewhere about Zhenhai and thence make his way to the great rear. As to whether Zhu Sheng reached Chongqing, and what became of him afterward, I no longer know.
This matter can go no further than here.

It was in the latter half of the twenty-eighth year that our superiors handed down an order to sanction Zhou Fohai. Although Zhou Fohai, moved thereto by the pair "Cheng and Peng," afterward entered into a connection with Mr. Dai Yunong of the "Juntong Bureau"—so much so that a special wireless set was designated by which he might communicate directly with Mr. Dai—still, the several working units of the "Juntong Bureau" at Nanjing, Shanghai, and Hangzhou had never to that day received the earlier order to cancel the sanction of Zhou Fohai.

How was this to be understood? I cannot in a line or two give any clear answer to such a question, for I may not wildly guess at a matter of such weight. Yet there must have been reasons on both sides. Say, for instance, that were another order canceling the sanction to be handed down, and it leaked out—would that not lay bare the truth and ruin a great affair? And then, should he really be sanctioned by parties each ignorant of the other's inside knowledge, what then? This was hard to speak of. From the working standpoint of my "Shanghai District," should the chance offer, we would of course carry it out as before.

Of the affair of Cheng and Peng's moving Zhou Fohai, what I know is limited, and I fear that to say too much, or to say what did not tally with the facts, would not be well either. Cheng believed in the Buddha, and died in Taiwan some years ago; Peng was a fickle turncoat, and was executed for another case fully thirty years since. I mean to look further into it, and leave it to be written in the fourth part of Nameless Heroes; for in the thirty-third year of the Republic there was still, between myself and Cheng and Peng, and Yang Xinghua (Zhou Fohai's brother-in-law), a secret connection there is no naming. For now let me first set down these two matters: Zhou Fohai's plotting, from the twelfth month of the twenty-ninth year to the second month of the thirtieth, to take over the Shanghai Special District Court and to get up the puppet Central Reserve Bank, and the action taken by my "Shanghai District."

The so-called "Shanghai Special District Court" was our government's "Shanghai French Concession Court" and "Shanghai International Settlement Court," under our government's jurisdiction. This was a most singular instance—there had been none before, nor will there be again—and it is needful here to explain it.

Though the Shanghai region had fallen, by the end of the twenty-ninth year the Shanghai Special District Court was still in our government's keeping; and Zhou Fohai, representing the Wang puppet regime, together with Li Shiqun and the rest under his direction, schemed to "take it over."

Why should there be a court of our government within the concessions? It was by agreement——The "Agreement Concerning the Shanghai International Settlement Special District Court" was signed at Nanjing on the twenty-seventh of the second month in the nineteenth year of the Republic, and noted as taking effect on the first of the fourth month of the nineteenth year of the Republic.
The full agreement ran to ten articles, of which the main contents were as follows:

One. From the day this agreement takes effect, all former regulations, agreements, exchanges of notes, and other instruments concerning the establishment of Chinese judicial organs within the Shanghai International Settlement shall be abolished.

Two. The Chinese government shall, in accordance with the Chinese laws and regulations touching the judicial system and with the provisions of this agreement, establish within the Shanghai International Settlement one district court and one branch high court; and all laws and regulations of China now in force, and such as shall hereafter be lawfully enacted and promulgated, whether substantive or procedural, shall alike apply to the said courts. As to the Yangjingbang Regulations and their appendices now in use, these shall be had regard to until the Chinese government shall itself enact and promulgate such regulations and appendices, and regard shall also be had to the provisions of this agreement. The civil and criminal judgments and rulings of the branch high court may, under Chinese law, be appealed to the Supreme Court of China.

Three. Whosoever is arrested by the Municipal Council police or by the judicial police shall, rest-days not counted, be delivered within twenty-four hours to the said courts established under this agreement for handling; failing delivery within the time, he shall forthwith be set at liberty. The above are but the chief points, not the whole text of the agreement. The one who signed for our government was Xu Mo, vice-minister of foreign affairs; the other signatory states were Brazil, represented by Di'ansi; the United States, by Yakebo; Britain, by Xu Lide; Norway, by Ge Longfu; the Netherlands, by He Longmen; and France, by Gan Gelin.
There is one point I am still not quite clear on, and I had never known that the Shanghai International Settlement, besides Britain, America, and France, had also Brazil, Norway, and the Netherlands.
The "Agreement for the Establishment of Chinese Courts in the Shanghai French Concession" was signed at Nanjing on the twenty-eighth of the seventh month in the twentieth year of the Republic.
The full agreement ran to fourteen articles, of which the main contents were as follows:

One. From the moment this agreement takes effect, the organ now established in the Shanghai French Concession, namely that called the Mixed Court, together with all regulations and usages pertaining thereto, shall be abolished.

Two. The Chinese government shall, in accordance with the Chinese laws and regulations touching judicial administration, establish within the Shanghai French Concession one district court and one branch high court. As to the judgments and rulings of the branch high court, the Supreme Court of China shall, under Chinese law, entertain appeals therefrom.

Three. The laws and regulations of China now in force, and such as shall hereafter be lawfully enacted and promulgated, shall alike apply to the said courts; and the administrative regulations of the concession shall likewise be had regard to. Four. All persons arrested within the concession shall, rest-days not counted, be delivered within twenty-four hours to the competent court; failing delivery within the time, they shall forthwith be set at liberty.
The above too are but the chief points, not the whole text of the agreement; those who signed for our government were Xu Mo and Wu Kunwu, and those who signed for France were Laigede and Ganggelan.

Both agreements for the establishment of courts in the two concessions were noted as running for a term of three years, extendable by three years upon the consent of both parties. Seeing that in the twenty-ninth year the concession courts still continued on, they must, I suppose, have been still in force under extension. (The chief points of the agreements are excerpted from "The Question of the Shanghai Concessions.")

In my nine years in Shanghai, first and last, I never could make out just what this business of Chinese courts within the two concessions was; and it was only after I had seen these two agreements that I learned there were so many niceties to it after all.

Yet before the enemy and the puppets set about seizing the concessions' Chinese courts, many of our working comrades, once arrested—though every one of them was a person protected under the law—were not delivered to the courts for trial at all, but were all "extradited" to the "Japanese gendarmerie" or to "No. 76."

As to the inside of how the enemy and puppets contrived to seize our courts in the Shanghai concessions, the "Diary of Zhou Fohai" lets one see the drift. Let me take the odd words and phrases of the "Diary of Zhou Fohai," string them together, and set out the facts in my own voice, as follows:
On the twenty-first of the tenth month of the twenty-ninth year, Zhou Fohai met with Li Shiqun to discuss the personnel question of "taking over" the Special District Court.

On the twenty-fifth of the tenth month, Zhou Fohai met with Li Shengwu to discuss the personnel of the Special District Court. Presently the Japanese garrison's Major-General Maeda, Colonel Yahagi of the Japanese General Staff, Staff Officer Sakata, and Wang Hanzhang and others held a meeting at Zhou's house on "taking over" the Special District Court.

On the second of the eleventh month, Zhou again conferred with the Japanese garrison's Major-General Maeda and the General Staff's Colonel Kagesa, Colonel Yahagi, and the rest on the question of "taking over" the French Concession court, the time being fixed for the fifth or sixth of the eleventh month.

On the third of the eleventh month, Zhou went again to Major-General Maeda's to discuss the matter of "taking over" the French Concession court. That afternoon the Japanese consul at Shanghai, Sone, called on Zhou Fohai to discuss the same question, but held that they must not press too hastily. That is to say, the Japanese side was not of one mind: the garrison was the more forward, the consulate the more temperate.

On the fourth of the eleventh month, Li Shiqun reported to Zhou Fohai that the French Concession authorities wished the "takeover" put off two days, and so it was decided to change it to the eighth, with no further delay. That evening Zhou Fohai went again to beg the help of the Japanese chief of staff, Sakurai.

On the afternoon of the fifth of the eleventh month, Li Shiqun reported to Zhou that the French police had put forward three conditions concerning the "takeover" of the court (the diary does not disclose their content), asking for a reply by three o'clock that afternoon, and Zhou at once gave his assent. That same evening Zhou telegraphed Wang Jingwei at Nanjing on the matter of negotiating the "takeover" of the Shanghai French Concession court.

On the evening of the seventh of the eleventh month, Li Shiqun reported to Zhou Fohai that the procedures for "taking over" the French Concession court on the eighth had been arranged and agreed upon with Japan and France both.

Toward eight in the morning of the eighth of the eleventh month, Zhou Fohai went to "No. 76" and, together with Li Shiqun, Major-General Maeda, and a good many others, waited quietly for news of the "takeover" of the French Concession court. At eleven he heard it was going smoothly; and by three in the afternoon Li Shiqun reported again that all was satisfactory.
Zhou records: "Liu Ruxiang brought the drafts of the Chinese declaration and the joint Japanese-French declaration on this matter, and consented to have them issued accordingly."

On the ninth of the eleventh month, Zhou Fohai wrote complacently in his diary: "Yesterday we took over the French Concession court, and today the premises of the Central Bank in the International Settlement (its original site); the hearts of the Shanghai people will surely be stirred. These two things I have labored over long, and only now have they come off—a joyful thing indeed."

On the evening of the seventeenth of the twelfth month, Chen Gongbo and Zhou Fohai discussed the question of "taking over" the International Settlement court. Chen thought it very easy; Zhou held it not so simple.
That day Zhou suddenly received a report that the Frenchman Duluo, who had handled the negotiations over the French Concession court, had abruptly been shot dead by our side.
Indeed, the shooting dead of the Frenchman Duluo was the doing of the "Shanghai District."

At the first, over the enemy and puppets' scheme to seize the Shanghai Special District Court, our superiors telegraphed the "Shanghai District" to collect the relevant intelligence and, besides, to contrive to check or wreck it. To collect intelligence was our proper duty; but as to checking or wrecking it, that was truly beyond us. For this reason, besides replying to our superiors that we would press harder to sanction the two men Zhou Fohai and Li Shiqun, we also asked for a ruling on whether we might —— the Frenchman Duluo, the Political Affairs Superintendent of the French Municipal Council, who was inclining to the enemy and puppets and playing go-between—which might perhaps have a repressive effect, and might, one could not say, slow the pace of their proceeding. Our superiors telegraphed their approval, and it was straightway handed to "New Group One" to carry out.

On the seventeenth of the twelfth month of the twenty-ninth year, the deputy leader of "New Group One" in charge of action, Comrade Huang Zhiyuan, leading Comrade Ding Xiaobao, the two of them, shot dead on the spot, before the door of No. 24 Baisaizhong Road in the French Concession, Duluo, the Political Affairs Superintendent of the French Municipal Council.

The French Concession's Chinese court was seized on the eighth; our shooting of Duluo was on the seventeenth—this because the going and coming of telegrams and the tracing and posting of the ground had held things up, so that we were a step late in the rhythm of it. Yet it could serve a chastening purpose all the same.

Here too there is no need to hide it: we had lived for many years now "on Chinese soil, within a foreign concession," and had in truth seen too much and tasted enough; say what one will, we could not put off a hatred of the foreign, above all toward that ruling stratum of the concessions who flaunted their power. Now that we had done this thing, we had not the least regret in it. Of course, a thing of this kind could only happen in the war-torn setting of that age.
Next to speak of Zhou Fohai's scheming to get up the puppet "Central Reserve Bank of China."
The Wang puppets aped Chongqing in everything, as though without doing so they could not be content.
At first the Wang puppets meant still to usurp the name "Central Bank"; later, feeling something amiss they could not name, they changed it to "Central Reserve Bank."
Of this matter too the diary of Zhou Fohai has some scattered, broken records; and now, using the same method as before, let me in my own voice set out the course of the facts, as follows:

On the twenty-fourth of the tenth month of the twenty-ninth year, Adviser Aoki of the Japanese embassy called on Zhou Fohai to discuss the "Central Bank" question, and Zhou said to Aoki: "The central authorities welcome Japanese cooperation, even guidance, but are unwilling to be placed under supervision," declaring firmly that they were unwilling to become a puppet bank.

On the evening of the twenty-fifth of the tenth month, Saionji and Inukai—the two who had dealt with Wang and Zhou ever since Hanoi—called on Zhou; Inukai produced a Sino-Japanese agreement on the "Central Bank" drawn up in advance by the Japanese side, in which the powers of the advisers were very large and the restrictions on Japan very strict. Of this Zhou Fohai wrote with feeling: "For the Japanese to hold on so tight, and yet to wish to realize the substance of Sino-Japanese amity, is truly not to be had." This is what is called being possessed by a devil.

From the twenty-sixth to the thirtieth of the tenth month, Zhou and a number of men discussed article by article the Sino-Japanese agreement on establishing a "Central Bank" put forward by the Japanese side, and conferred more than once with Inukai on amending its content.
On the afternoon of the second of the eleventh month, Zhou Fohai met with Kimura Ichitarō and engaged him as an adviser to the "Central Bank."

On the fourth of the eleventh month, Liu Ruxiang proposed "taking over" the premises of the former Central Bank at Shanghai. Inukai, together with Aoki, again met Zhou Fohai for a final discussion of the Sino-Japanese agreement on the "Central Bank," with the result still not wholly agreed.
On the seventh of the eleventh month, Liu Ruxiang reported to Zhou that the former premises of the Shanghai Central Bank could be "taken over" within the week.

On the ninth of the eleventh month—already spoken of in the passage above—Zhou Fohai counted it a joyful thing to be able to "take over" the former premises of the Central Bank. What there was in this to be joyful over, I do not know.

On the fourteenth of the eleventh month, Kagesa came to tell Zhou Fohai that he would accompany him to Tokyo, both to press the Japanese authorities to recognize the Nanjing puppet regime, and, as to the many knots to be untied over the "Central Bank," it was settled that Ueda and others should go along, the better to do side-work for the "Central Bank."

On the fifteenth of the eleventh month, Zhou Fohai summoned the two, Qian Shucheng and Liu Ruxiang, inquired into the course of "taking over" the old Central Bank premises, and directed Qian and Liu to press their contacts with the Shanghai financial and commercial worlds, above all the four great companies (Sun Sun, Dah Sun, Wing On, Sincere), so as to make them accept the "new legal tender" (the reserve notes).

On the twentieth of the eleventh month, Zhou Fohai, in Tokyo, went to the Bank of Japan to call on its governor, Yūki. Yūki, a magnate of Japanese finance, told Zhou that the Bank of Japan would cooperate closely with the "Central Bank." Zhou then went to the printing bureau of the Japanese cabinet to inspect the rush-printing of notes for the puppet "Central Reserve Bank."

At noon on the twenty-first of the eleventh month, Aoki gave a banquet to draw together leading figures of the Japanese financial world with Zhou; there came Yūki of the Bank of Japan, Ōkubo of the Specie Bank, Ishii of the Hypothec Bank, and some twenty others.

On the twenty-fifth of the eleventh month, after Zhou returned to Shanghai, he at once summoned Qian Shucheng, Liu Ruxiang, and the rest to inquire in detail into the state of the "Central Bank's" preparations. Such was his solicitude.

From the first to the seventh of the twelfth month, Zhou Fohai discussed severally with his subordinates the matter of issuing the new currency. This so-called "new currency" was the "reserve notes"—also called the "new reserve notes"—soon to be issued by the puppet "Central Reserve Bank"; its purpose was of course to replace the fabi still circulating in the fallen zone.
During this time Zhou was also arranging the internal personnel of the puppet "Central Reserve Bank," but disputes kept breaking out, and he had much ado to level them.

On the seventeenth of the twelfth month, the Wang puppet Executive Yuan in session passed the "Provisional Measures for the Regulation of Currency," and the president, vice-president, directors, and supervisors of the puppet "Central Bank" (note: that is, the "Central Reserve Bank").

Zhou Fohai, at the puppet Ministry of Finance, signed with Hidaka, representing the Japanese side, a "Memorandum on Sino-Japanese Cooperation in the Establishment of the Central Bank." It was decided to issue a declaration on currency policy on the twentieth; to hold the first meeting of directors on the twenty-first; and on the sixth of the first month of the thirtieth year the puppet "Central Reserve Bank" formally opened.

On the twenty-first of the twelfth month, it was rumored that the Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation at Shanghai would shortly post its board, raising the exchange rate and pressing down paper money, the intent seeming to be to counter the "Central Reserve" new notes. Zhou Fohai held this move quite unwise, as it would do the Wang puppets no harm but would inflict a great loss on Chongqing. This shows plainly enough that the one who struck at the "fabi" and thereby harmed the people should, of course, be reckoned the arch-criminal Zhou Fohai.
On the ——th of the twelfth month, the American consul-general at Shanghai called on Zhou Fohai, hoping the puppet "Central Reserve Bank" would postpone its establishment.

On the afternoon of the twenty-seventh of the twelfth month, Zhou Fohai led a party on a round of inspection of the puppet "Central Reserve Bank"; all was in readiness, and Zhou was greatly gratified.

The "Diary of Zhou Fohai" has only the one volume for the twenty-ninth year; the affair of the puppet "Central Reserve Bank's" opening for business was already a matter of the very beginning of the thirtieth year.

Mr. Dai was especially sensitive to the financial and economic questions of the fallen zone. I do not know whether this was a far-sighted vision of his own in the leading of the work, or a policy he was charged to carry out, or whether it held yet some other meaning.

When I served at the "Tianjin Station," I was continually receiving the order to sanction Wang Shiying, three or four times in all. Wang Shiying was then director-general of the finance department of the North China puppet regime and concurrently governor of the "Federal Reserve Bank." After I was transferred to Hanoi, Comrade Sun Dacheng of the Kang Corps made a special trip from Tianjin to Beiping to see to this case, but it is a pity that neither of us accomplished the task.

In the twenty-eighth year, a working group of the Kang Corps led by Sun Dacheng at last sanctioned Cheng Xigeng, superintendent of the Tianjin Maritime Customs and concurrently general manager of the "Federal Reserve Bank."

This time it was Zhou Fohai and the rest within the Wang regime who were getting up the puppet "Central Reserve Bank." In the earlier stage of its brewing—that is, when we had just come to learn of this intelligence—Mr. Dai had already sent down instructions, seeming to have gained by then a still deeper intelligence, ordering the "Shanghai District," besides actively laying lines to sanction Zhou Fohai, to sanction as well the high personnel already fixed upon for it.
