Thereafter our superiors sent several more telegrams, ordering the "Shanghai District" to press its several brigades and groups strictly to deal a wrecking blow at the puppet "Central Reserve Bank" soon to appear.

This work, rather than say it was all carried out as our superiors required, one had better say that in every point it fell short of being well done. Not only that: it drew, on the contrary, a great calamity down on many innocent people.

The targets of sanction ought to have been the bank's high personnel—the several directors and supervisors, the heads of business, and the like; that might perhaps have produced some awing effect. In the event, by the reports of the several brigades and groups, what they did reached only the middle personnel. This was because the basic grasp of the work was not sufficiently full, and because of the want of upper-social connections.

By the report of the "Third Action Brigade": on the third of the first month of the thirtieth year, a party led by Ye Dongshan sanctioned, in Lane 174 of Kaiziěr Road, one Ji Mingyuan, a special commissioner of the puppet "Central Reserve Bank."

By the report of "New Group One": on the seventeenth of the fourth month of the thirtieth year, a party under Zhao Jiaxin and others of the group set out and sanctioned, at No. 73 in Lane 391 of Xi'aixiansi Road, one Zhang Yonggang, chief accountant of the Shanghai branch of the puppet "Central Reserve Bank."

By the report of the "Seventh Action Brigade": on the twenty-second of the fourth month of the thirtieth year, a party under He Fengxiang and others, members of the Brigade, set out and sanctioned, at the Zhongnan Hotel on Avenue Edward VII, one Li Dingmo, an auditor of the Shanghai branch of the puppet "Central Reserve Bank."

The above are three cases of action, carried out severally by three units. There were besides two cases of sabotage, the target being the Shanghai branch of the puppet "Central Reserve Bank." In truth, though the head office bore in name the seat of Nanjing, its main body was still at Shanghai.

Both the first and the second were carried out by the "Third Action Brigade," the comrades setting out being Dong Wei, Tian Jielin, Lin Zhencheng, and several more. The first was in the last third of the first month of the thirtieth year; three explosive devices in all were thrown—one gave off smoke but did not go off, and the other two made not the slightest stir. Great pains were spent and grave risk run, and the result fell far short of what was hoped.

The second was on the twentieth of the second month of the thirtieth year, more than a month after the bank had opened, and seemingly falling just at the old New Year. Those who set out were again the original men of the Third Brigade, some six or seven in all; they carried, severally, a good many devices of different sizes and forms, the target being still the puppet "Central Reserve Bank" set up on the Bund.

Beforehand we had not failed to consider it: the explosives to be thrown must, as required, "go off," but must not be allowed any killing power—it was enough that they be like great firecrackers. For we knew that, with such small things alone, one could by no means destroy a great bank, but might very likely implicate many innocents; and the little clerks seated within the counters, and the customers standing without, would be bound to bear the first brunt of it—how could that be allowed? What we wanted was the shock sent out by the noise.
That the first only gave off smoke and made no report was precisely because it had not been properly set.

This second time it worked at last; one cannot say it did not throw things into disorder, yet the enemy and puppets' secret police, having long foreseen this move, had planted many hidden watchers in advance. The comrades of the Third Brigade had no time to withdraw; several were arrested one after another, Lin Zhencheng among them. Afterward more were arrested in succession.
In truth, done thus, the wrecking power it gave the enemy and puppets was very limited, and might well be judged no method worth admiring.
Not long after these two disorder-sowing operations, "No. 76" took a bloody revenge—an atrocity conscienceless, base, and shameless.

Was this Zhou Fohai's notion? or the currying of favor and claiming of merit by Li Shiqun and the rest? It seems they were all tarred with the one brush. They took guardsmen and action men of the "Special Operations Headquarters" and made up on the spot a "plainclothes assault squad," who, carrying severally short guns, light machine guns, and other weapons, loaded onto two truckloads, front and rear answering each other, burst into the concessions and drove straight to the door of our side's Bank of China.

This pack leapt down from the trucks, drew up in formation, and marched with great show into the bank, giving a shout and bidding the clerks within, great and small, gather together and fall into a line.

The bank's staff, pressed by circumstance, dared not disobey, and so in twos and threes they crowded to the front gate, none of them knowing what was about to happen—some, indeed, laughing at it in blank bewilderment.
In that very instant a great fusillade broke out, the light machine guns raking in bursts; bodies of flesh and blood fell at the sound, the dead and wounded past counting.

Besides the Bank of China, another establishment met with much the same; the several score of innocents, dead or wounded, were all lower staff of the banks, and every one of them ought to be numbered among the sacrificed of the war of resistance.
This affair the newspapers of the day all carried, and for several days running; and afterward the periodicals too had much comment upon it.

In the two years from the autumn of the twenty-eighth year to the winter of the thirtieth, our behind-the-lines action in Shanghai—the fierce blows dealt at the enemy and puppets' hawks and hounds, at the great traitors and arch-villains, and at the opportunist small fry—did indeed produce an awing effect. Its influence spread not only our renown far through the fallen zone, but heartened the spirit of the people toward the whole future of our resistance.

Yet because the striking force could not be brought to bear unceasingly and ever strengthened, and because we lacked effective means to check and guard against the enemy and puppets' counter-thrust, our organization suffered destruction time and again, while the arrogance of the enemy and puppets waxed by the day more unbridled.

From the beginning of the thirtieth year, the Wang puppet "Special Operations Headquarters," in league with the "Shanghai Japanese gendarmerie," each designated an authorized unit, whose sole business was to visit upon my "Shanghai District" a thoroughgoing search and arrest.

Perilous as our circumstances thus were, we understood deeply where our duty lay, and dared not, nor would, shrink back; by an incomplete count, in the ten months that followed we still brought off more than sixty cases of action and sabotage, an average of one every five days; and thereby the comrades arrested, and so sacrificed, grew by degrees more numerous.

At this juncture, to add to our strength, we set about actively reorganizing the "First Action Brigade," a body of deep latent power that had shown very little. On this question I consulted Brother Liu Yuanshen, the assistant secretary, who had already been ordered to a training course but had not yet set out, and asked him, under the style of acting commander of the "First Action Brigade," to lend the "Shanghai District" a hand for two months more. Moved by a sense that he could not in honor decline, Brother Yuanshen at once gladly consented. Little did I think that, through my own want of foresight in this arrangement, Brother Yuanshen would be sold by some petty villain and fall into the enemy's hands. Though in his bonds he suffered every kind of torment, he still held fast to his integrity, kept the organization safe, and set up a model of a might that would not bend—a hero and a brave man indeed.

By the end of the tenth month, on a night of frequent air-raid alarms, through a want of steadiness on my part, and a further string of mistaken judgments, I actually walked into the net and fell into the trap—to my deep shame.

At first they did not know that I was the "Shanghai District" chief; later, by finding men again and again to identify me, my true identity was at last laid bare. Things having come to this, what I could still hold to was that I must on no account lose the dignity due to one who had once been head of a thousand men. As for how they meant to deal with me, that was their affair.
Nevertheless, the behind-the-lines work in Shanghai under the leadership of the "Juntong Bureau" did not, because of my dereliction and capture, come to a stop.
